ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: 3 days of watery diarrhea requiring frequent toilet use.
- Symptoms (onset/duration/severity/agg/alg): Started ~3 days ago. Loose, watery stools 6–7 times/day. Crampy, intermittent lower abdominal pain localized to the left side. Vomiting at onset but has stopped. Felt feverish at symptom onset (patient-noted temperature), currently afebrile. Weakness/shakiness and reduced appetite. Able to tolerate fluids (soups, smoothies). Symptoms impairing daily activities and work.
- Past medical history: Asthma (uses an inhaler; reportedly controlled).
- Medications / allergies: Inhaler only. No other medications reported. No allergies mentioned.
- Family / social history: Lives with wife and two children. One child had vomiting (did not have diarrhea). Works as an accountant. Non-smoker. Does not drink alcohol.
- Vital signs / exam findings: No measured vitals documented. No physical exam findings recorded; clinician planned conservative management and did not perform/r eport exam/vitals.
- Labs / imaging: None mentioned; no stool studies done yet.
- Exposure history: Ate a Chinese takeaway ~4 days ago. No other known sick contacts except one child who vomited.
- Other relevant: No blood in stool or vomit. No ongoing fever reported at visit. Has been continuing to attend work despite symptoms.

V: Ischemic colitis: Left-sided abdominal pain and diarrhea can occur with ischemia of the sigmoid colon; typically occurs in older patients or those with vascular risk — less likely here given acute diarrheal illness and systemic symptoms suggesting infection.
I:
Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus, rotavirus): Common cause of acute watery diarrhea, vomiting early, systemic features (fever, malaise), often self-limited over several days — matches watery stools, vomiting at onset, household contact vomiting, recent onset.
Bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli): Food-associated onset after takeaway; can cause frequent watery/bloody stools, abdominal cramps, fever and systemic symptoms. Time course (food 4 days ago, symptoms 3 days) fits many bacterial pathogens.
Staphylococcal or Bacillus cereus toxin-mediated food poisoning: Often presents with rapid-onset vomiting predominant (hours) rather than multi-day watery diarrhea; less consistent with 3-day diarrheal course but possible depending on exposure.
N: Colonic neoplasm: Unlikely to present acutely with 3 days of watery diarrhea and vomiting; would be lower on differential unless chronic or bleeding symptoms develop.
D: Electrolyte disturbance/dehydration: Secondary complication from ongoing diarrhea and decreased intake causing weakness/shakiness — more a consequence than primary cause.
Lactose or food intolerance: Could cause watery diarrhea and crampy pain but less likely with acute febrile prodrome and vomiting; unlikely to explain systemic symptoms.
I2: Medication-induced diarrhea (e.g., antibiotic-associated C. difficile): Patient denies recent antibiotics; inhaler unlikely to cause this presentation — low probability.
Foodborne toxin as above (iatrogenic/intoxication overlap): e.g., preformed toxins from improperly stored food could cause acute gastroenteritis.
C: Congenital malrotation or bowel anomalies: Unlikely to present de novo at this age with typical infectious features.
A: Allergic gastroenteritis/food allergy: Typically causes vomiting, cramps, sometimes diarrhea shortly after exposure; less likely to present with fever and household spread.
T: Traumatic bowel injury: No history of trauma; not applicable.
E: Endocrine/metabolic (thyroid, adrenal): Hyperthyroidism can cause increased bowel motions but would be chronic and associated with other features; adrenal crisis could cause abdominal pain/weakness but less likely in this otherwise well patient.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute onset watery diarrhea, vomiting at onset, systemic symptoms (felt feverish, weakness), household contact (child) with vomiting, short self-limited course over days — all classic for viral gastroenteritis.
supporting_evidence: 3 days of watery, loose stools 6–7 times/day
Vomiting at the start of symptoms
Patient felt febrile at symptom onset
Able to tolerate fluids and symptoms improving in vomiting (typical course)
opposing_evidence: Localized left-sided abdominal pain could suggest a focal pathology (e.g., diverticulitis) rather than diffuse viral enteritis
Recent takeaway meal raises possibility of bacterial foodborne illness

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Bacterial foodborne gastroenteritis (food poisoning — e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, enterotoxigenic E. coli)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: History of eating a Chinese takeaway ~4 days ago with symptom onset ~3 days ago is compatible with incubation periods for several bacterial pathogens; presents with crampy abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea and initial vomiting.
supporting_evidence: Ate Chinese takeaway ~4 days prior to presentation
Fever at onset and systemic symptoms (weakness, shakiness)
Crampy abdominal pain and frequent watery stools
opposing_evidence: No blood in stool (some bacterial enteritis can cause bloody diarrhea, though not always)
Household transmission (child vomiting) more typical for viral pathogens
Patient is maintaining fluids and symptoms appear consistent with self-limited course

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Left lower quadrant crampy pain with fever and change in bowel habits can indicate diverticulitis. However, classic diverticulitis more commonly causes localized tenderness, sometimes constipation or low-grade fever rather than high-frequency watery diarrhea; patient age not provided but presentation is possible.
supporting_evidence: Localized left-sided lower abdominal crampy pain
Change in bowel habit and systemic symptoms
opposing_evidence: High-frequency watery diarrhea (6–7/day) and initial vomiting are more typical of infectious gastroenteritis than diverticulitis
No localized peritonism, no documented abdominal exam or focal tenderness reported
No prior history of diverticular disease mentioned

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Inflammatory bowel disease flare (e.g., ulcerative colitis or Crohn's colitis)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Could produce diarrhea, abdominal pain and systemic symptoms, but new-onset acute presentation over 3 days without blood in stool or prior history makes this less likely.
opposing_evidence: No history of chronic bowel disease or prior flares
Absence of blood or chronicity; temporal relation to possible food exposure and household contact favors infectious cause
